'''''Jacobaea maritima''''', commonly known as '''silver ragwort''', is a [[perennial plant]] species in the genus ''[[Jacobaea]]'' in the family [[Asteraceae]], native to the [[Mediterranean region]]. It was formerly placed in the genus ''[[Senecio]]'', and is still widely referred to as '''''Senecio cineraria'''''; see the list of synonyms (right) for other names.

It is widely cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]] for its white, [[felt]]-like [[trichome|tomentose]] leaves; in [[horticultural]] use, it is also sometimes called '''dusty miller''', a name shared with several other plants that also have silvery tomentose leaves, including ''[[Centaurea cineraria]]'' and ''[[Silene coronaria]]''.

==Description==
[[File:Fly at flower.jpg|thumb|left|Flowers, [[Port-Cros National Park]], France]]

Silver Ragwort is a very [[white]]-[[trichome|wooly]], heat and drought tolerant [[evergreen]] [[subshrub]] growing to {{convert|0.5|–|1|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall. The stems are stiff and woody at the base, densely branched, and covered in long, matted grey-white to white hairs. The leaves are [[pinnate]] or pinnatifid, {{convert|5|–|15|cm}} long and {{convert|3|–|7|cm}} broad, stiff, with oblong and obtuse segments, and like the stems, covered with long, thinly to thickly matted with grey-white to white hairs; the lower leaves are [[Petiole (botany)|petiolate]] and more deeply lobed, the upper leaves sessile and less lobed.

The tomentum is thickest on the underside of the leaves, and can become worn off on the upper side, leaving the top surface [[Glossary of botanical terms#glabrous|glabrous]] with age. The flowers are yellow, daisy-like in dense [[Head (botany)|capitula]] {{convert|12|–|15|mm}} in diameter, with central [[disc floret]]s surrounded by a ring of 10–13 ray florets, and enclosed in a common whorl of [[bract]]s at the base of the [[Head (botany)|capitulum]]. The seeds are cylindrical [[achenes]].<ref name=Flora>Interactive Flora of NW Europe: [http://wbd.etibioinformatics.nl/bis/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=4074 ''Senecio cineraria''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120402001220/http://wbd.etibioinformatics.nl/bis/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=4074 |date=2012-04-02 }}</ref><ref name=Blamey>Blamey, M. & Grey-Wilson, C. (1989). ''Flora of Britain and Northern Europe''. {{ISBN|0-340-40170-2}}</ref><ref name=Huxley>Huxley, A., ed. (1992). ''New RHS Dictionary of Gardening''. Macmillan {{ISBN|0-333-47494-5}}.</ref>

==Distribution==
''Jacobaea maritima'' is [[native plant|native]] to the western and central Mediterranean region, in northwest Africa (Morocco, northern Algeria, Tunisia), southern Europe (Spain, Gibraltar, southern France including Corsica, Italy including Sardinia and Sicily, Malta, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, Albania, Montenegro, Serbia, North Macedonia, and Greece), and the far west of Asia (Turkey). It occurs primarily on cliffs and rocky coastal sites, more rarely inland.<ref name=EUROMED/><ref name=GRIN/><ref name=Blamey/>

It is also [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] further north in Europe (north to Great Britain and Ireland, where occurring mainly in mild coastal areas<ref name=Flora/><ref name=Blamey/>) and locally in [[North America]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=SECI2| title=PLANTS Profile, ''Senecio cineraria'' DC.|access-date=2008-02-27|author= Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS)|authorlink=Natural Resources Conservation Service|work=The PLANTS Database|publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]}}</ref>

==Ecology==
As with many other densely tomentose plants, the tomentum, or hair-like pieces on the stems and leaves, is used by some species of [[bee]]s (e.g. ''[[Anthidium manicatum]]'' and ''[[Anthidium oblongatum]]'' in [[Megachilidae]]) for nest-building.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Shane R. Miller, Robert Gaebel, Randall J. Mitchell, and Mike Arduser|author2=University of Akron|title=Occurrence of two species of Old World bees, ''Anthidium manicatum'' and ''A. oblongatum'' (Apoidea: Megachilidae), in northern Ohio and southern Michigan|journal=The Great Lakes Entomologist|volume=35|issue=1|pages=65–69|url=http://www3.uakron.edu/biology/mitchell/pdfs/Miller%20et%20al%202002.pdf|accessdate=2008-03-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090205040824/http://www3.uakron.edu/biology/mitchell/pdfs/Miller%20et%20al%202002.pdf|archive-date=2009-02-05|url-status=dead}}</ref>

[[Hybrid (biology)|Hybrids]] are known with ''[[Jacobaea erucifolia]]'' and ''[[Jacobaea vulgaris]]. The'' ''J. vulgaris'' variant is fertile producing a wide range of intermediate progeny.<ref name=Flora/><ref name=Blamey/>

==Cultivation and uses==

''Jacobaea maritima'' is widely used in horticulture for its silvery foliage. It is winter-hardy in [[Hardiness zone|USDA Zones 8-10]], tolerating winter temperatures down to -12 to -15 °C,<ref name=Huxley/><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://nature.jardin.free.fr/arbrisseau/ft_senecio_cin.html|title=Cinéraire maritime, Senecio cineraria, Séneçon cinéraire|website=nature.jardin.free.fr|accessdate=May 1, 2023}}</ref> tolerant of light shade but preferring full sun.<ref name=Huxley/> In colder areas it is grown as an [[annual plant]]. Many [[cultivar]]s have been selected for particularly dense silvery tomentum, such as 'Cirrus', 'New Look', 'Ramparts', 'Silverdust', 'Silver Filigree', and 'White Diamond'.<ref name=Huxley/> It has been recommended in North America for its fire resistance,<ref name=plumas>{{cite web|url=http://plumasfiresafe.org/Documents/treenote17.fire%20resits%20plant.3.pdf|title=Tree Notes|accessdate=2008-03-02|author=J. Knutson-Pedersen|authorlink=California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection|date=July 2005|work=Fire Safe Landscaping|publisher=[[Plumas County, California|Plumas Fire Safe Council]]|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080510144511/http://www.plumasfiresafe.org/Documents/treenote17.fire%20resits%20plant.3.pdf|archivedate=2008-05-10}}</ref> resistance to [[browsing (herbivory)|browsing]] by [[deer]],<ref name=tamu>{{cite web|url=http://aggie-horticulture.tamu.edu/plantanswers/publications/deerbest.html|title=Coping with the deer by the use of deer resistant plants.|accessdate=2008-02-29|author=F. W. Appleton|authorlink=Cooperative extension service|date=2003-09-29| publisher=[[Texas A&M University]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://aggie-hort.tamu.edu/plantanswers/web.html|title=PLANTanswers|website=aggie-hort.tamu.edu|accessdate=May 1, 2023}}</ref> and its [[halophyte|salt tolerance]].<ref name=yorkcounty>{{cite web|url=http://www.yorkcounty.gov/vce/progareas/hort/pubs/Salt%20Tolerant%20Plants%20w%20ltrhead.pdf |title=Salt Tolerant Plants for Water-front Applications |accessdate=2008-03-03 |author=York County Office |authorlink=York County, Virginia |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20071024172937/http://www.yorkcounty.gov/vce/progareas/hort/pubs/Salt%20Tolerant%20Plants%20w%20ltrhead.pdf |archivedate=2007-10-24 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The [[cultivar]] 'Silver Dust' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Senecio cineraria'' 'Silver Dust'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/353991/Jacobaea-maritima-Silver-Dust/Details | accessdate = 7 September 2020}}</ref>

Confusion in the horticultural trade exists between ''J. maritima'' and ''[[Centaurea cineraria]]'', which has resulted in confusion regarding which cultivars pertain to either species, which has also resulted in much confusion in photographs of these species on the internet.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hind |first1=Nicholas |last2=Hashi |first2=Mayumi |last3=Brown |first3=Andrew |date=March 2022 |title=1009. CENTAUREA CINERARIA: Compositae |journal=Curtis's Botanical Magazine |language=en |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=35–54 |doi=10.1111/curt.12431 |issn=1355-4905|doi-access=free }}</ref>
